blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized asthma self-management education, written action planning, and escalation of care
stem: A nurse reviews a provider-developed written asthma action plan with a client. Which explanation best describes the purpose of the plan?

options.A: Give individualized daily-control instructions and predefined steps for worsening symptoms, including when to call the provider or seek emergency care.
options.B: Use the same medication steps at each symptom level so the client can follow a fixed sequence without adjusting actions to current symptoms or peak flow.
options.C: Focus on trigger avoidance and the routine medication schedule, while leaving decisions about worsening symptoms to unplanned calls with the provider.
options.D: Use symptom or peak-flow zones mainly to document severity for follow-up, while postponing treatment changes until the next scheduled appointment.

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC guidance states that everyone with asthma needs an individualized Asthma Action Plan created with a health care provider. CDC organizes the plan into zones for doing well, worsening asthma, and medical alert, with predefined actions that include controller or reliever medicines and escalation when symptoms do not improve. Current NHLBI guidance describes the asthma action plan as a written treatment plan created with the provider that identifies triggers, how to recognize an attack and what to do, which medicines to take and when, when to call the provider or go to the emergency room, and emergency contacts. B is incorrect because an asthma action plan is individualized and changes actions according to asthma status rather than applying the same steps at every symptom level. C is incomplete because the plan is specifically intended to guide actions during worsening symptoms instead of relying on an unplanned call for each decision. D is incorrect because the zones guide active treatment and escalation; they are not merely documentation categories while treatment is deferred until a scheduled visit.
educational_objective: Use an individualized written asthma action plan to guide daily control, early treatment of worsening symptoms, and timely escalation to provider or emergency care.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI/NIH); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Living with Asthma; Asthma Treatment and Action Plan; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: CDC Living with Asthma dated 2026-05-04; current NHLBI Asthma Treatment and Action Plan resource rechecked 2026-08-20; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: CDC 'Living with Asthma' dated May 4, 2026: Key points/Asthma Action Plans state everyone with asthma needs an individual plan created with a health care provider; Green Zone gives daily controller actions when doing well; Yellow Zone identifies worsening symptoms and adds reliever medicine/continued controller therapy with reassessment; Red Zone identifies medical-alert findings and directs additional prescribed medicine, provider contact, and hospital care if not improving. NHLBI 'Asthma Treatment and Action Plan': provider and patient create a written plan identifying triggers, recognition/action for attacks, medicines and timing, when to call the provider or go to the emergency room, and emergency contacts. NHLBI 'Asthma Attack': follow the action plan, use reliever medicine when symptoms begin, and seek urgent/emergency care based on severity and response. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Management of Care supports client education, follow-up planning, coordination, and escalation of care.
source_claim_supported: Current federal CDC/NHLBI guidance directly supports individualized written asthma action plans that translate daily control and worsening symptoms into predefined medication/self-management and escalation actions. NCSBN supports the nursing education and care-coordination construct.
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: provide and reinforce client education, coordinate follow-up and continuity of care, recognize changes requiring escalation, and collaborate with health-care providers.

correction_summary: Original Q1923 had a uniquely longest correct answer (126 characters versus 74-108) and easily eliminated distractors. The item was rebuilt with four closely balanced, clinically plausible explanations of an asthma action plan. The correct answer now requires integrating individualized daily control, worsening-symptom actions, medications, and escalation rather than selecting the longest or most obviously comprehensive option. Independent post-fetch reread found no unresolved source, clinical, currentness, ambiguity, cueing, blueprint, or second-answer conflict.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly matches CDC/NHLBI descriptions of an individualized written plan covering daily control, worsening symptoms, medicines, and escalation.
option_audit.B: Plausible protocol misconception; incorrect because plan actions vary with the client's current zone/symptoms rather than using the same steps at each level.
option_audit.C: Plausible partial-purpose distractor; trigger avoidance and routine medicines belong in the plan, but it also gives predefined actions for worsening asthma.
option_audit.D: Plausible monitoring-focused distractor; zones guide active treatment/escalation, not just documentation for a later appointment.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on only/all/always/never/must-type absolute wording.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths: A 151, B 153, C 150, D 146 characters; the correct answer is not the longest and choices are tightly balanced.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives explain a plausible purpose or use of the same written action plan in parallel form.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: Independent adversarial reread found no defensible second answer. C is intentionally partly true but omits the defining worsening-symptom action component; B and D conflict with individualized zone-based action. A is uniquely best.
